# Spec-side black-box experiments (spec side only)

Small images the spec side runs in fwtest to confirm facts in
`docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (M0c). The spec cites them only as E-n and their
result; nothing here leaves `harness/`. They are written from the JieLi
SDK's register map and, where the SDK has no bit meanings, from the vendored
emulator's model (`exp.h` says which). Each confirms how fwtest presents the
board, not how real hardware behaves.

- Build: `sh harness/spec-experiments/build.sh` (the pinned toolchain
  container; writes `images/` and `images/SHA256SUMS`).
- Run: `sh harness/spec-experiments/run.sh OUT` rebuilds, compares with the
  committed images, and runs `experiments.suite` against this checkout's
  fwtest (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS, R-SPEC-4). The golden files are the results.
- Not part of fwtest: `harness/ci.sh` leaves this folder out of the fwtest
  build context, and the image-publishing workflow ignores it.

| ID | Image | What it shows (the golden files hold the numbers) |
|----|-------|---------------------------------------------------|
| E-1 | `e1-boot` | At entry: r0 = 0x01C7FC00, r2..r15, sp, usp, ssp, icfg, psr and cnum all 0 (r1 not observable: used as the pointer). The block at r0: first word 0x01C7FC40, the other 15 zero. The code window past the image reads 0xFFFFFFFF (erased flash), also 4 KiB further. A written word reads back at 0x01C7FDFC, 0x01CFFFFC, 0x01F3FFFC and 0x0407FFFC. |
| E-2 | `e2-console` | Word writes to DBG_MSG append their 4 bytes, low byte first. A byte or halfword write appends 4 bytes too: the written bytes merged into the last word written (console "abcd12:\nX2:\nYZ:\nend\n"). |
| E-3 | `e3-timers` | TIMER5 PRD 600: an interrupt (63) every 100 µs; TIMER4 advanced 2400 counts (24 MHz) between two. TIMER0 prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: an interrupt (4) every 1 ms; its CON read in the handler is 0x8021 (bit 15 pending). TTMR with PRD 1234: an interrupt (3) every 10 ms. ILAT_SET bit 0: interrupt 120 once. Counts at 52.3 ms (the capture came late, below): 523, 52, 5, 1. |
| E-4 | `e4-core1` | With core 1's entry in the word at 0x01C7FFF8, setting C1_CON bit 3 starts core 1 there; cnum reads 0 on core 0 and 1 on core 1; core 1 ran on stacks it set itself. |
| E-5 | `e5-lcd` | SPI1 bytes with PC8 low are commands, high data. CASET/RASET/RAMWR with RGB565 pixels high byte first, by single bytes (BUF) and by DMA (ADR, CNT from RAM) both draw. INVON and DISPOFF leave the captured picture as written. A software reset (0x01) clears it to black. |
| E-6 | `e6-matrix` | The log gives each fwtest key's (column, row) and each encoder's two contacts and their order (clockwise: the second contact closes first). Matches the table in the spec. |
| E-7 | `e7-leds` | LED line PA9, PA10, PH6, PH9 lights, in the selected column, the LED of the key at row 1, 2, 3, 4 of that column. |
| E-8 | `e8-adc` | Channel 4 reads the pot (900 at the start, then the script's 300, 0, 1023); channel 3 reads 640; every other channel 512. |
| E-9 | `e9-audio` | A half of 128 words (64 frames) every 1.451 ms after the first at 1.459 ms (44 117.6 frames a second). The first half to finish is half 0; the half just finished is CON0 bit 15 inverted. A sample is the word shifted right by 8, clamped to 16 bits: 0x007fffff gives 32767, 0xff800000 -32768, 0x01000000 32767, 0x00000080 0. |
| E-10 | `e10-faults` | No fault reaches sources 0-2 (handlers count 0), before and after writing EMU_CON 0x001F010F, EMU_SSP/USP limits excluding the stacks, DBG_EN 0x003F0030. Misaligned word loads give the bytes at the address (RAM+1: 0x04030201; code+1: 0x14131211); halfword loads at RAM+1 and +3 give 0x0100 and 0x0302 (the lowest address bit ignored); a word stored at RAM+9 lands in bytes 9-12. The addresses come from a volatile word: with constant addresses the compiler split the RAM accesses into byte accesses. Unmapped 0x00ABCDEC reads 0, and after a write still 0. A code-window write reads back unchanged. Signed and unsigned 1234/0 give 0; 1234%0 (as compiled) gives 1234. EMU_CON and the limits read back; EMU_MSG 0; DBG_EN 0 (unmodelled). The console is "E10\nend\n": writes to DBG_WR_EN and DBG_MSG_CLR between the two words left it alone. |
| E-11 | `e11-undefined` | A call to a function whose first halfword is 0xFFFF: the run ends as a fault ("cannot decode"), after the marker, with no handler run. |
| E-12 | `e12-badjump` | A call to 0x00ABCDEE: fwtest runs the zeros it reads there for 1024 instructions, then ends the run as a fault ("the pc left every memory"); no handler ran. |
| E-13 | `e13-timer-ack` | TIMER0, prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: 100 periods are 2 400 100 TIMER4 ticks with the acknowledge first in the handler (1 tick after entry) and 2 408 160 with it 82 ticks after entry; CNT reads 5 just before the acknowledge, 0 just after. The periphery model restarts the count and the period at every CON write. |
| E-14 | `e14-undefined-inline` | A marker store, then the halfword 0xFFFF in the same straight-line code: the run ends as a fault at the start of that code (the pc of main's first instruction), and the marker was never written. |
| E-15 | `e15-spi1-irq` | SPI1 CON bit 13 and source 16. CON reads 0x8000 before any write. Bit 13 never set, or written clear: no interrupt for a 2-byte DMA or a BUF byte. Bit 13 set: one interrupt each (the handler acknowledges with `CON |= 0x4000`); CON reads 0xA000. A DMA done with bit 13 set and the source off in ICFG, then CON written 0 and the source turned on: taken once. Before the SR-3 fix (vendor patch 0002, fwtest 0.2.0) a CON write could not clear bit 13, so the clear steps counted too. |
| E-16 | `e16-lcd-frame` | One CNT write of 115 200 bytes from RAM draws a whole frame (rows 0-119 red, 120-239 blue), pixel (0,0) green and (239,239) white in place. |
| E-17 | `e17-adc-irq` | SARADC CON bit 5 and source 24: a start of channel 4 with bit 5 gives one interrupt, without it none, also right after one with it. In the handler RES 900, CON 0x4F0; after the acknowledge (CON = 0x40) CON 0x40; after a start without bit 5, 0x4D0. |

## 7. Audio output (M4)

### HW-43: The audio link's registers
- Fact: `JL_ALNK0` is at `0x00012E00`: `CON0` +0, `CON1` +4, `CON2` +8,
  `CON3` +12, `ADR0` to `ADR3` at +16 to +28, `LEN` +32. Its interrupt
  source is 11.
- Sources: SDK `WL82.h` lines 664-677; SDK `hwi.h` line 50
  (`IRQ_ALNK_IDX` 11).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK)
- Needed by: M4

### HW-44: The output buffer and sample format, in fwtest
- Fact: In fwtest the output plays from a buffer in RAM at the address in
  `JL_ALNK0->ADR3`: two halves, one after the other, each of `LEN` 32-bit
  words. Words alternate left, right, left, right (`LEN` / 2 stereo frames
  a half). Write each sample as a 24-bit signed value in the word's low
  bits, sign-extended: fwtest's WAV takes the whole word shifted right
  arithmetically by 8 bits, clamped to -32768..32767. Which bits the chip
  uses is Q-9.
- Sources: E-9: with `LEN` 128 each half played 64 frames; the words
  `0x007FFFFF`, `0xFF800000`, `0x01000000` and `0x00000080` came out as
  32767, -32768, 32767 and 0, and a left ramp written as value × 256 came
  out as the values; HARNESS ("audio.wav").
- Standing: confirmed (E-9)
- Needed by: M4

### HW-45: The output's rate and halves
- Fact: In fwtest, writing `JL_ALNK0->CON0` with bit 11 set starts the
  output with half 0; a half lasts `LEN` / 2 frames of 544 / 24 MHz each:
  44 117.6 frames a second (fwtest's WAV header says 44 100). Writing
  `CON0` without bit 11 stops it. `CON0` bit 15 reads the half now
  playing, so the half that has just finished, and is free to refill, is
  that bit inverted. Each finished half sets `CON2` bit 7 and raises
  interrupt source 11 (while `CON0` bit 11 is set and the source is
  enabled); writing `CON2` with bit 3 set clears it.
- Sources: E-9: with `LEN` 128, halves finished 1.451 ms apart (the first
  at 1.459 ms), the first to finish was half 0, and `CON0` bit 15 inverted
  named it each time; RE `docs/io/03-audio-dac.md` §5.3 (the meaning of
  `CON2` bit 7 and of `CON0` bit 15 in this block); HARNESS ("audio.wav").
- Standing: confirmed (RE, E-9)
- Needed by: M4

  check-hardware-spec.py [FILE] [--base REV]

Every entry is a `### HW-n: title` heading followed by the fields
`- Fact:`, `- Sources:`, `- Standing:` and `- Needed by:`, each non-empty.
It fails on:
  - a missing or empty field, or a field it doesn't know;
  - an ID used twice, or an open question (`**Q-n.`) numbered twice;
  - a standing that isn't `confirmed ...`, `emulator-only ...`,
    `other chip (SDK63)` or `superseded by HW-n` (an entry that exists);
  - an `other chip` entry whose sources don't cite SDK63 (another JieLi
    chip's SDK; such an entry is never confirmed for the FM-1's chip);
  - a confirmed entry whose sources name nothing independent: it must cite
    SDK, RE, DS, PANEL, MAN or an experiment E-n (HARNESS, the spec side's own
    description of fwtest, and the emulator model don't count);
  - an experiment E-n cited but not listed in
    harness/spec-experiments/README.md (checked only where harness/ is on
    disk; a clean folder skips that part and says so);
  - code: a fenced code block anywhere in the file;
  - history: against REV (default: the merge base with origin/main, when
    there is one and the file existed there), an entry that has gone, or
    one whose fact text changed. A corrected fact gets a new ID and the old
    entry is marked superseded; IDs are never reused or renumbered.
"""
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SPEC = os.path.join(ROOT, "docs", "HARDWARE-SPEC.md")
EXPERIMENTS = os.path.join(ROOT, "harness", "spec-experiments", "README.md")
FIELDS = ("Fact", "Sources", "Standing", "Needed by")
HEAD = re.compile(r"^### (HW-(\d+)): (\S.*)$")
FIELD = re.compile(r"^- ([A-Z][a-z]+(?: by)?):\s*(.*)$")
SOURCE_KEYS = re.compile(r"\b(SDK|RE|DS|PANEL|MAN|E-\d+)\b")

## Open questions

What isn't known, or is known only from material the spec may not use. A
spec request can turn one into a fact.

- **Q-1. Other RAM on the chip.** Whether the chip has RAM at `0x01F00000`
  and `0x04000000` (HW-7), how much, and whether it can be used. The SDK's
  layout names a cache RAM at `0x01F20000` and an external SDRAM window at
  (its release, Q-11; its cache and protection set-up); whether a
  peripheral source enabled on both cores interrupts both. The `corex2`
  block has per-core counters (words 0x80 to 0x8F, SDK `csfr.h` lines
  119-134) whose meaning the SDK doesn't state. Settled by a probe on real hardware.
- **Q-18. Memory seen across the cores on the chip.** Whether main RAM is
  cached, and whether a plain store by one core is seen by the other's
  next load without `csync` or a cache operation (HW-65). Settled by a
  probe on real hardware.
- **Q-19. The block moves' write-back forms on the chip.** What
  `{list} = [rN++]`, `{list} = [--rN]` and their stores leave in the base
  (fwtest: rN + 4n, rN - 4n), which wins when such a form's base is also
  in its list, and what an empty list does (HW-66). The toolchain's
  compiler was not seen to emit them. Settled by a probe on real
  hardware.
- **Q-20. MIDI output on the chip.** Which UART and pin drive the
  SMK-37's MIDI OUT jack, and its port set-up (fixed pin pair or an output
  channel of `JL_IOMAP`; drive); how its TRS socket is wired (type A or B);
  whether the SMK-37 has the FM-1's chip; whether the FM-1's board brings
  UART1's transmit pin anywhere; which `CON0` bit enables the transmit
  interrupt (bit 2 on the chips SDK63 covers, HW-75); whether, after a DMA, the pending means the transfer has been
  read from RAM or the last stop bit has left the pin; whether the
  transmit DMA needs a 4-byte aligned address or length; what writing
  `TXCNT` does while a transfer is still going; how `BUF` and the DMA mix.
  Settled by a datasheet or a probe on real hardware (an SMK-37 and an
  FM-1).

## 19. Flash storage (SR-9, M7)

Completes section 8 for SR-9. HW-76 to HW-79 are the chip and its flash
part, HW-80 and HW-81 the FM-1's flash layout and what the boot chain and
the update path need, HW-82 fwtest as pinned (0.5.0). Open: Q-21 to Q-24.

### HW-76: The flash part's identity
- Fact: In fwtest the flash chip answers the JEDEC ID read (`0x9F`) with
  `0x85 0x60 0x14`. The Puya P25Q80H datasheet gives exactly that ID for
  that part (Puya's manufacturer ID `0x85`; `0x60 0x14`, 8 Mbit, so
  1 MiB). Whether the FM-1 carries that part is known only from the
  emulator, whose model says it answers as real units do; no allowed
  source names the part, and FM-1-RE says only that the firmware reads the
  ID and takes the capacity from it. Read the ID on the chip and, if it
  differs, look up that part's datasheet before relying on HW-77's times
  (Q-21). A firmware that reads the ID at start-up and checks it can
  refuse to write to a part it doesn't know.
- Sources: PUYA p. 54 (table "ID Definitions": RDID `85 60 14`); E-22
  (fwtest's answer); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §1 (the ID read, capacity
  as 2^n); the emulator model (the part on real units).
- Standing: emulator-only (the part on the FM-1); confirmed (PUYA) that
  the ID is the P25Q80H's
- Needed by: M7

### HW-77: The P25Q80H's sizes, times and endurance
- Fact: The P25Q80H, from its datasheet: 1 MiB; programming only clears
  bits (1 to 0), and only an erase sets them back to 1. Erase units: a
  256-byte page (`0x81`), a 4 KiB sector (`0x20`), a 32 KiB block
  (`0x52`), a 64 KiB block (`0xD8`), the whole chip (`0x60` or `0xC7`);
  program: up to 256 bytes within one 256-byte page (`0x02`). Times,
  typical / maximum: page program 2 / 3 ms; page, sector, 32 KiB, 64 KiB
  and whole-chip erase each 8 / 12 ms; status register write 8 / 12 ms.
  Endurance 100 000 program/erase cycles; data retention 20 years. An
  erase or program can be suspended (`0x75` or `0xB0`) and resumed
  (`0x7A` or `0x30`): the suspend takes effect within 30 µs, and an erase
  makes progress only if at least 200 µs (a program 100 µs) pass between
  a resume and the next suspend. While suspended, the array outside the
  sector being erased or the page being programmed can be read. The
  requirement: wait for the end of each operation by reading the status
  register (HW-78), never by a fixed delay, and plan for the maximum
  times.
- Sources: PUYA p. 1 and p. 4 (100K cycles, 20-year retention), p. 11
  (AC table: tPP, tPE, tSE, tBE1, tBE2, tCE, tW, tESL, tPSL, notes 4 and
  5), p. 21-22 (command table), p. 40-43 (erase and page program), p. 55
  (suspend and resume).
- Standing: confirmed (PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-78: The P25Q80H's command rules and the busy state
- Fact: From the datasheet: a write enable (`0x06`, which sets the status
  register's WEL bit) must come before every program, erase and status
  register write; without it the command is ignored, and WEL clears again
  when the operation ends. A program or erase starts when chip select goes
  high, and only if it goes high at a byte boundary (after the eighth bit
  of a byte); otherwise the command is rejected. A page program whose
  bytes run past the end of the 256-byte page wraps round to the page's
  first byte (bytes before the start address are then written); of more
  than 256 bytes only the last 256 are kept; fewer than 256 change only
  the bytes sent. Status register 1 (`0x05`): bit 0 WIP (1 while a
  program, erase or status write is in progress), bit 1 WEL, bits 2-6
  block protect BP0-BP4 (non-volatile: an erase or program in a protected
  area is not executed), bit 7 SRP0. While WIP is 1 the chip ignores
  array reads (`0x03`, `0x0B` and the dual and quad reads) and the ID
  reads; reading the status register works throughout.
- Sources: PUYA p. 18 (chip select at a byte boundary; array access
  ignored during a program, erase or status write), p. 25-26 (status
  register bits, block protect), p. 31-32 (reads rejected while busy),
  p. 40 (erase needs WEL, starts on chip select high), p. 43 (page
  program, the wrap, the last 256 bytes), p. 54 (ID read not decoded
  while busy).
- Standing: confirmed (PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-79: Code, interrupts, core 1 and audio while the flash is busy
- Fact: On the chip one SPI NOR flash holds everything, and the code
  window reads it (FM-1-RE). While the firmware works the flash directly,
  from its first command until the operation ends (WIP 0, HW-78), nothing
  may be fetched or read from the code window: no code, no constant
  tables or strings, no interrupt handler, nothing on core 1. The JieLi
  SDK's example of direct flash access says so: everything between
  entering and leaving that mode, code, data and constants, must be in
  RAM, and nothing may be printed when the system runs from flash; and
  the chip ignores array reads while busy (HW-78), so the window cannot be
  served then. The stock firmware keeps its flash routines and several
  interrupt handlers in RAM (FM-1-RE). So: put the routine that works the
  flash, and everything it calls and reads, in RAM; for its whole length
  either keep interrupts masked, or have every handler that can run, and
  everything it reaches, in RAM; and keep core 1 off the window too
  (stopped, or running from RAM). How the window's own controller hands
  the flash over to SPI0 and back on the chip is Q-22. Audio: the output
  plays its halves from RAM by itself (HW-44, HW-45), so it keeps playing
  as long as each half is refilled in time. A 4 KiB erase can take 12 ms,
  about 530 frames at 44 117.6 frames a second, more than a half lasts
  unless `LEN` is over about 1 060 words. To keep the audio going through
  an erase, either the refill handler and the synthesis it runs are in RAM
  and interrupts stay on, or the erase is cut into pieces with suspend and
  resume (HW-77) so the window can be used between them, or the output is
  muted and the gap accepted. fwtest checks none of this today (HW-82).
- Sources: SDK `apps/common/example/peripheral/flash/flash_register/main.c`
  lines 9-22 and 39-46 (the comments around the direct-access section:
  code, data and constants in RAM; no printing when running from flash);
  PUYA p. 18, p. 31-32 (array reads ignored while busy); RE
  `docs/io/09-storage.md` (one flash holds everything; the code window
  reads it) and `docs/io/01-boot.md` §1 (flash routines and interrupt
  handlers RAM-resident); HW-45 (the half's length).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-80: The FM-1's flash layout, and the region a firmware may use
- Fact: On an FM-1 with M-VAVE's firmware, the 1 MiB flash is laid out
  as follows (chip offsets):
  - `0x00000`-`0x03FFF`: the boot area: a header, the second-stage loader
    from `0x000A0` (which the mask ROM loads), the loader's configuration
    from `0x038D0`. Never erase or write it: the chip boots from it.
  - `0x04000`-`0x93FFF`: the app area: a file table, then the app and its
    configuration, encrypted with the chip's key (HW-81). The update
    package's flash image covers `0x00000`-`0x93FFF`.
  - `0x94000`-`0xE8FFF` (340 KiB): the stock firmware's key-value store
    ("VM"). The update path also stages its loader in "the VM/loader
    flash area" (FM-1-RE; where in it, not stated).
  - `0xE9000`-`0xE9FFF`: Bluetooth information ("BTIF").
  - `0xEA000`-`0xFBFFF` (72 KiB, 18 sectors): the stock firmware's user
    patch storage ("USR"); the update package carries a `USR` entry.
  - `0xFC000`-`0xFEFFF` (12 KiB): unused.
  - `0xFF000`-`0xFFFFF`: holds a per-unit key and address (`key_mac`).
    Never erase it: nothing can restore it. The SDK's packaging tool also
    reserves a flash's last 4 KiB by default.
  So a firmware's own storage must stay out of the boot area, out of its
  own image, and out of the last 4 KiB, and should stay out of the
  Bluetooth sector. In particular "the chip's last 64 KiB" includes the
  last sector: end a store at `0xFEFFF` at the latest. Where our firmware
  sits on the chip, and so what is free, is set when M9 packages it; until
  then the stock layout's USR region, `0xEA000`-`0xFBFFF`, is the region
  its owner's firmware already uses for user data and is the natural
  place, kept in one definition. FM-1-RE adds that its free regions have
  not been validated as safe for writes from outside the stock firmware,
  and whether an update rewrites the USR or VM region is not known
  (Q-24). In fwtest the whole chip past the image is erased and free
  (HW-5, HW-82).
- Sources: RE `docs/architecture.md` §2 ("Flash layout", from the update
  package's file table) and §3 (the mask ROM loads the loader from
  `0xA0`); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §3 (the loader reads the file table's
  section tags); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §3 and §6 (the VM store; the
  free regions not validated); RE `docs/io/11-ota-protocol.md` (the
  package's entries, among them `flash.bin` and `USR`; the loader staged
  in the VM/loader area); SDK `cpu/wl82/tools/isd_config_rule.c` lines
  106 and 306-334 (the last 4 KiB reserved; reserved regions and whether
  a download erases, keeps or protects each).
- Standing: confirmed (RE, SDK)
- Needed by: M7, M9

### HW-81: The code window on the chip differs from fwtest's
- Fact: On the chip:
  - The app area from `0x04000` is encrypted with the chip's key, and the
    window shows it decrypted; the stock firmware scrambles data it
    writes below its app area's end so that it reads back through the
    window. Plain data written over SPI0 inside that area therefore
    reads back changed through the window.
  - The stock window starts at chip offset `0x04120` (the app's first
    byte after the file table): window address `0x02000000 + n` is chip
    offset `0x4120 + n`. In fwtest it is `0x4000 + n` (HW-5).
  - The stock firmware synchronises the instruction cache after a
    program, so the window may keep showing old bytes after a change
    (Q-22).
  The requirement: address the store by chip offset, and read it back with
  the flash's read command (`0x03`) over SPI0, not through the code
  window; then the same code reads the same bytes on the chip and in
  fwtest.
- Sources: RE `docs/architecture.md` §2 (the window as flash offset −
  `0x4120` + `0x02000000`; the app area encrypted with the chip key from
  `0x4000`); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §1 (the cache synchronised after a
  program; writes below the encrypted region's end scrambled); HW-5.
- Standing: confirmed (RE)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-82: The flash chip in fwtest 0.5.0
- Fact: In fwtest as pinned (0.5.0), beyond HW-47: an SPI0 byte takes no
  emulated time of its own (64 bytes cost only the instructions that send
  them); an erase or program completes when its command does, and the
  status register's WIP bit is never 1, so a firmware's wait for WIP ends
  at its first read; a page program sent without a write enable still
  writes (the chip ignores it, HW-78); bytes programmed past the end of a
  256-byte page go on into the next page (the chip wraps them to the
  page's start); programming clears bits only, as on the chip; a 4 KiB
  erase clears its aligned sector and a 64 KiB erase its aligned block;
  reading through the window during or after a flash operation always
  works. Not modelled: the 32 KiB block erase (`0x52`), the page erase
  (`0x81`), the chip erase, suspend and resume, block protection. The
  flash persists between runs only through files: `--flash FILE` gives the
  chip's starting bytes (the image is then written at `0x4000` again) and
  `--flash-out` saves the whole chip at the end of the run, whatever its
  outcome. A run that ends (`--ms`) stops with the flash as it is then;
  with operations instantaneous, that can't fall inside one. fwtest's
  next version is to model the busy times, the page wrap and the write
  enable, and a power cut during an operation (HARNESS.md will say when).
- Sources: E-22 (64 bytes in 45 TIMER4 ticks; erase, then one status read
  with WIP 0; `F0 0F AA FF` then `3C` ×4 gave `30 0C 28 3C`; a program
  without WREN wrote; "ABCD" at `0x800FE` put "CD" at `0x80100`; the erase
  extents); HARNESS ("The flash chip", `--flash`, `--flash-out`); the
  emulator model (the commands not modelled).
- Standing: confirmed (E-22)
- Needed by: M7

  that part (Puya's manufacturer ID `0x85`; `0x60 0x14`, 8 Mbit, so
  1 MiB). Whether the FM-1 carries that part is known only from the
  emulator, whose model says it answers as real units do; no allowed
  source names the part, and FM-1-RE says only that the firmware reads the
  ID and takes the capacity from it. Read the ID on the chip and, if it
  differs, look up that part's datasheet before relying on HW-77's times
  (Q-21). A firmware that reads the ID at start-up and checks it can
  refuse to write to a part it doesn't know.
- Sources: PUYA p. 54 (table "ID Definitions": RDID `85 60 14`); E-22
  (fwtest's answer); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §1 (the ID read, capacity
  as 2^n); the emulator model (the part on real units).
- Standing: emulator-only (the part on the FM-1); confirmed (PUYA) that
  the ID is the P25Q80H's
- Needed by: M7

### HW-77: The P25Q80H's sizes, times and endurance
- Fact: The P25Q80H, from its datasheet: 1 MiB; programming only clears
  bits (1 to 0), and only an erase sets them back to 1. Erase units: a
  256-byte page (`0x81`), a 4 KiB sector (`0x20`), a 32 KiB block
  (`0x52`), a 64 KiB block (`0xD8`), the whole chip (`0x60` or `0xC7`);
  program: up to 256 bytes within one 256-byte page (`0x02`). Times,
  typical / maximum: page program 2 / 3 ms; page, sector, 32 KiB, 64 KiB
  and whole-chip erase each 8 / 12 ms; status register write 8 / 12 ms.
  Endurance 100 000 program/erase cycles; data retention 20 years. An
  erase or program can be suspended (`0x75` or `0xB0`) and resumed
  (`0x7A` or `0x30`): the suspend takes effect within 30 µs, and an erase
  makes progress only if at least 200 µs (a program 100 µs) pass between
  a resume and the next suspend. While suspended, the array outside the
  sector being erased or the page being programmed can be read. The
  requirement: wait for the end of each operation by reading the status
  register (HW-78), never by a fixed delay, and plan for the maximum
  times.
- Sources: PUYA p. 1 and p. 4 (100K cycles, 20-year retention), p. 11
  (AC table: tPP, tPE, tSE, tBE1, tBE2, tCE, tW, tESL, tPSL, notes 4 and
  5), p. 21-22 (command table), p. 40-43 (erase and page program), p. 55
  (suspend and resume).
- Standing: confirmed (PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-78: The P25Q80H's command rules and the busy state
- Fact: From the datasheet: a write enable (`0x06`, which sets the status
  register's WEL bit) must come before every program, erase and status
  register write; without it the command is ignored, and WEL clears again
  when the operation ends. A program or erase starts when chip select goes
  high, and only if it goes high at a byte boundary (after the eighth bit
  of a byte); otherwise the command is rejected. A page program whose
  bytes run past the end of the 256-byte page wraps round to the page's
  first byte (bytes before the start address are then written); of more
  than 256 bytes only the last 256 are kept; fewer than 256 change only
  the bytes sent. Status register 1 (`0x05`): bit 0 WIP (1 while a
  program, erase or status write is in progress), bit 1 WEL, bits 2-6
  block protect BP0-BP4 (non-volatile: an erase or program in a protected
  area is not executed), bit 7 SRP0. While WIP is 1 the chip ignores
  array reads (`0x03`, `0x0B` and the dual and quad reads) and the ID
  reads; reading the status register works throughout.
- Sources: PUYA p. 18 (chip select at a byte boundary; array access
  ignored during a program, erase or status write), p. 25-26 (status
  register bits, block protect), p. 31-32 (reads rejected while busy),
  p. 40 (erase needs WEL, starts on chip select high), p. 43 (page
  program, the wrap, the last 256 bytes), p. 54 (ID read not decoded
  while busy).
- Standing: confirmed (PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-79: Code, interrupts, core 1 and audio while the flash is busy
- Fact: On the chip one SPI NOR flash holds everything, and the code
  window reads it (FM-1-RE). While the firmware works the flash directly,
  from its first command until the operation ends (WIP 0, HW-78), nothing
  may be fetched or read from the code window: no code, no constant
  tables or strings, no interrupt handler, nothing on core 1. The JieLi
  SDK's example of direct flash access says so: everything between
  entering and leaving that mode, code, data and constants, must be in
  RAM, and nothing may be printed when the system runs from flash; and
  the chip ignores array reads while busy (HW-78), so the window cannot be
  served then. The stock firmware keeps its flash routines and several
  interrupt handlers in RAM (FM-1-RE). So: put the routine that works the
  flash, and everything it calls and reads, in RAM; for its whole length
  either keep interrupts masked, or have every handler that can run, and
  everything it reaches, in RAM; and keep core 1 off the window too
  (stopped, or running from RAM). How the window's own controller hands
  the flash over to SPI0 and back on the chip is Q-22. Audio: the output
  plays its halves from RAM by itself (HW-44, HW-45), so it keeps playing
  as long as each half is refilled in time. A 4 KiB erase can take 12 ms,
  about 530 frames at 44 117.6 frames a second, more than a half lasts
  unless `LEN` is over about 1 060 words. To keep the audio going through
  an erase, either the refill handler and the synthesis it runs are in RAM
  and interrupts stay on, or the erase is cut into pieces with suspend and
  resume (HW-77) so the window can be used between them, or the output is
  muted and the gap accepted. fwtest checks none of this today (HW-82).
- Sources: SDK `apps/common/example/peripheral/flash/flash_register/main.c`
  lines 9-22 and 39-46 (the comments around the direct-access section:
  code, data and constants in RAM; no printing when running from flash);
  PUYA p. 18, p. 31-32 (array reads ignored while busy); RE
  `docs/io/09-storage.md` (one flash holds everything; the code window
  reads it) and `docs/io/01-boot.md` §1 (flash routines and interrupt
  handlers RAM-resident); HW-45 (the half's length).
- Standing: confirmed (SDK, RE, PUYA)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-80: The FM-1's flash layout, and the region a firmware may use
- Fact: On an FM-1 with M-VAVE's firmware, the 1 MiB flash is laid out
  as follows (chip offsets):
  - `0x00000`-`0x03FFF`: the boot area: a header, the second-stage loader
    from `0x000A0` (which the mask ROM loads), the loader's configuration
    from `0x038D0`. Never erase or write it: the chip boots from it.
  - `0x04000`-`0x93FFF`: the app area: a file table, then the app and its
    configuration, encrypted with the chip's key (HW-81). The update
    package's flash image covers `0x00000`-`0x93FFF`.
  - `0x94000`-`0xE8FFF` (340 KiB): the stock firmware's key-value store
    ("VM"). The update path also stages its loader in "the VM/loader
    flash area" (FM-1-RE; where in it, not stated).
  - `0xE9000`-`0xE9FFF`: Bluetooth information ("BTIF").
  - `0xEA000`-`0xFBFFF` (72 KiB, 18 sectors): the stock firmware's user
    patch storage ("USR"); the update package carries a `USR` entry.
  - `0xFC000`-`0xFEFFF` (12 KiB): unused.
  - `0xFF000`-`0xFFFFF`: holds a per-unit key and address (`key_mac`).
    Never erase it: nothing can restore it. The SDK's packaging tool also
    reserves a flash's last 4 KiB by default.
  So a firmware's own storage must stay out of the boot area, out of its
  own image, and out of the last 4 KiB, and should stay out of the
  Bluetooth sector. In particular "the chip's last 64 KiB" includes the
  last sector: end a store at `0xFEFFF` at the latest. Where our firmware
  sits on the chip, and so what is free, is set when M9 packages it; until
  then the stock layout's USR region, `0xEA000`-`0xFBFFF`, is the region
  its owner's firmware already uses for user data and is the natural
  place, kept in one definition. FM-1-RE adds that its free regions have
  not been validated as safe for writes from outside the stock firmware,
  and whether an update rewrites the USR or VM region is not known
  (Q-24). In fwtest the whole chip past the image is erased and free
  (HW-5, HW-82).
- Sources: RE `docs/architecture.md` §2 ("Flash layout", from the update
  package's file table) and §3 (the mask ROM loads the loader from
  `0xA0`); RE `docs/io/01-boot.md` §3 (the loader reads the file table's
  section tags); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §3 and §6 (the VM store; the
  free regions not validated); RE `docs/io/11-ota-protocol.md` (the
  package's entries, among them `flash.bin` and `USR`; the loader staged
  in the VM/loader area); SDK `cpu/wl82/tools/isd_config_rule.c` lines
  106 and 306-334 (the last 4 KiB reserved; reserved regions and whether
  a download erases, keeps or protects each).
- Standing: confirmed (RE, SDK)
- Needed by: M7, M9

### HW-81: The code window on the chip differs from fwtest's
- Fact: On the chip:
  - The app area from `0x04000` is encrypted with the chip's key, and the
    window shows it decrypted; the stock firmware scrambles data it
    writes below its app area's end so that it reads back through the
    window. Plain data written over SPI0 inside that area therefore
    reads back changed through the window.
  - The stock window starts at chip offset `0x04120` (the app's first
    byte after the file table): window address `0x02000000 + n` is chip
    offset `0x4120 + n`. In fwtest it is `0x4000 + n` (HW-5).
  - The stock firmware synchronises the instruction cache after a
    program, so the window may keep showing old bytes after a change
    (Q-22).
  The requirement: address the store by chip offset, and read it back with
  the flash's read command (`0x03`) over SPI0, not through the code
  window; then the same code reads the same bytes on the chip and in
  fwtest.
- Sources: RE `docs/architecture.md` §2 (the window as flash offset −
  `0x4120` + `0x02000000`; the app area encrypted with the chip key from
  `0x4000`); RE `docs/io/09-storage.md` §1 (the cache synchronised after a
  program; writes below the encrypted region's end scrambled); HW-5.
- Standing: confirmed (RE)
- Needed by: M7

### HW-82: The flash chip in fwtest 0.5.0
- Fact: In fwtest as pinned (0.5.0), beyond HW-47: an SPI0 byte takes no
  emulated time of its own (64 bytes cost only the instructions that send
  them); an erase or program completes when its command does, and the
  status register's WIP bit is never 1, so a firmware's wait for WIP ends
  at its first read; a page program sent without a write enable still
  writes (the chip ignores it, HW-78); bytes programmed past the end of a
  256-byte page go on into the next page (the chip wraps them to the
  page's start); programming clears bits only, as on the chip; a 4 KiB
  erase clears its aligned sector and a 64 KiB erase its aligned block;
  reading through the window during or after a flash operation always
  works. Not modelled: the 32 KiB block erase (`0x52`), the page erase
  (`0x81`), the chip erase, suspend and resume, block protection. The
  flash persists between runs only through files: `--flash FILE` gives the
  chip's starting bytes (the image is then written at `0x4000` again) and
  `--flash-out` saves the whole chip at the end of the run, whatever its
  outcome. A run that ends (`--ms`) stops with the flash as it is then;
  with operations instantaneous, that can't fall inside one. fwtest's
  next version is to model the busy times, the page wrap and the write
  enable, and a power cut during an operation (HARNESS.md will say when).

- Standing: confirmed (E-22)

content.content:
# The FM engine's patch format, version 1

A patch is everything the FM engine (M5, `firmware/src/fm.h`) needs to
play a sound: 112 bytes, each field one byte, or two bytes little-endian,
so a patch can be saved to flash (M7) and shared (the app) as it is,
without conversion. `tools/fm_patch.py` writes and checks patches in this
format (its `encode` and `problems`), and `fm_patch_valid()` in
`firmware/src/fm_play.c` checks them the same way. The test patches are
defined once, in `tools/fm_patch.py`, and generated into
`firmware/src/patches.c`; they are our own (R-FM-7).

## Layout

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Values |
|-------:|------:|-------|--------|
| 0 | 2 | magic | `F` `M` (0x46, 0x4D) |
| 2 | 1 | version | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | length | 112, the whole patch |
| 4 | 12 | name | printable ASCII (32 to 126), padded with 0 |
| 16 | 1 | algorithm | 1 to 10 ("The algorithms", docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M5) |
| 17 | 1 | feedback | 0 (none) to 7, on the algorithm's feedback operator |
| 18 | 1 | flags | bit 0: mono; the other bits 0 |
| 19 | 1 | glide | a time code (below); 0: none. Mono only |
| 20 | 1 | transpose | signed semitones, -24 to 24 |
| 21 | 1 | pitch depth | signed semitones that a pitch level of 127 means, -48 to 48 |
| 22 | 3 | pitch rates | time codes: P0 to P1, P1 to P2 (then held), and to P3 on release |
| 25 | 4 | pitch levels | P0 (at note on) to P3, signed, -127 to 127 |
| 29 | 3 | reserved | 0 |
| 32 | 6 x 13 | operators | operator 1 first (below) |
| 110 | 2 | check sum | Fletcher-16 of bytes 0 to 109: low byte the first sum, high byte the second, each mod 255 |

Each operator, 13 bytes from its first:

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Values |
|-------:|------:|-------|--------|
| 0 | 1 | mode | 0: a ratio of the note's frequency; 1: a fixed frequency |
| 1 | 2 | frequency | ratio x 256 (256 is 1.0, up to 255.996), or a fixed frequency in quarter hertz |
| 3 | 1 | detune | signed cents, -100 to 100 |
| 4 | 1 | level | 0 (off) to 127; gain 2^((level - 127) / 8) |
| 5 | 1 | velocity | sensitivity 0 to 7: at 7, velocity 0 is 8 octaves (48.2 dB) quieter than 127, in proportion between |
| 6 | 4 | rates | time codes: attack, decay 1, decay 2, release |
| 10 | 3 | levels | 0 to 127, as level: the attack's peak, the level after decay 1, the level held |

## Units

- **A time code** t, 0 to 127, is 2^(t / 8) ms, from 1 ms to 60.1 s: the
  time a stage takes over its whole range. The attack's range is a gain
  of 0 to 1; the decays' and the release's is 16 octaves (96.3 dB); the
  pitch envelope's 254 levels. A stage that moves only part of its range
  takes that part of the time.
- **A level** step is 2^(1/8), 0.753 dB; 127 is 0 dB.
- **An operator's index**: a modulator at full level moves its carrier's
  phase by 4 pi radians at the most (fm.c, `MOD_SHIFT`); level 103 (a gain
  of 1/8) is index pi/2.
- **Feedback** k (1 to 7) moves the operator's phase by up to
  pi / 2^(7 - k) times the mean of its last two outputs.

## Versions

Version 1 is the first (M5). A reader must refuse a patch with another
magic, version or length, a bad check sum or a field out of range: it
never guesses. A later version will keep the first four bytes' meaning,
so any reader can tell a patch it doesn't know from a damaged one, and
will say here what changed.
#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Vendors three crates of the public emulator upstream, at a pinned commit,
# into vendor/emulator/, applies the patches in vendor/emulator/patches/, and
# checks every file against vendor/emulator/SHA256SUMS, whose own SHA-256 is
# the tree hash below (PROVENANCE P-7). Spec side only: vendor/emulator/ is
# left out of clean folders, and --fetch refuses to run in one.
#
#   tools/fetch-emulator.sh --verify   check the committed files (default,
#                                      offline; SKIP when vendor/emulator/
#                                      isn't on disk, as in a clean folder)
#   tools/fetch-emulator.sh --fetch    re-download them from the pinned commit,
#                                      apply the patches, then verify
#
# The fetch is a blob-less clone with a sparse checkout of exactly the paths
# in UPSTREAM_PATHS, so nothing else in that repository reaches the disk.
# To move to another commit: change UPSTREAM_COMMIT, run --fetch in a spec
# folder, rewrite SHA256SUMS (--sums), update TREE_SHA256 and UPSTREAM.md,
# and log it in PROVENANCE.md, all in one pull request.
set -eu

UPSTREAM_URL=https://github.com/joakimeriksson/fm1-emu.git
UPSTREAM_COMMIT=43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f
UPSTREAM_PATHS="
/LICENSE
/Cargo.toml
/crates/fm1-isa/
/crates/fm1-core/
/crates/fm1-soc/
"
# SHA-256 of vendor/emulator/SHA256SUMS: one hash for the whole tree.
TREE_SHA256=9b3e9a17577c416aa8f2f58d3dc1f8fa81e3b8f77752efc0f656439f4b2b8d8e

toolUseResult.stdout:
# The FM engine's patch format, version 1

A patch is everything the FM engine (M5, `firmware/src/fm.h`) needs to
play a sound: 112 bytes, each field one byte, or two bytes little-endian,
so a patch can be saved to flash (M7) and shared (the app) as it is,
without conversion. `tools/fm_patch.py` writes and checks patches in this
format (its `encode` and `problems`), and `fm_patch_valid()` in
`firmware/src/fm_play.c` checks them the same way. The test patches are
defined once, in `tools/fm_patch.py`, and generated into
`firmware/src/patches.c`; they are our own (R-FM-7).

## Layout

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Values |
|-------:|------:|-------|--------|
| 0 | 2 | magic | `F` `M` (0x46, 0x4D) |
| 2 | 1 | version | 1 |
| 3 | 1 | length | 112, the whole patch |
| 4 | 12 | name | printable ASCII (32 to 126), padded with 0 |
| 16 | 1 | algorithm | 1 to 10 ("The algorithms", docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M5) |
| 17 | 1 | feedback | 0 (none) to 7, on the algorithm's feedback operator |
| 18 | 1 | flags | bit 0: mono; the other bits 0 |
| 19 | 1 | glide | a time code (below); 0: none. Mono only |
| 20 | 1 | transpose | signed semitones, -24 to 24 |
| 21 | 1 | pitch depth | signed semitones that a pitch level of 127 means, -48 to 48 |
| 22 | 3 | pitch rates | time codes: P0 to P1, P1 to P2 (then held), and to P3 on release |
| 25 | 4 | pitch levels | P0 (at note on) to P3, signed, -127 to 127 |
| 29 | 3 | reserved | 0 |
| 32 | 6 x 13 | operators | operator 1 first (below) |
| 110 | 2 | check sum | Fletcher-16 of bytes 0 to 109: low byte the first sum, high byte the second, each mod 255 |

Each operator, 13 bytes from its first:

| Offset | Bytes | Field | Values |
|-------:|------:|-------|--------|
| 0 | 1 | mode | 0: a ratio of the note's frequency; 1: a fixed frequency |
| 1 | 2 | frequency | ratio x 256 (256 is 1.0, up to 255.996), or a fixed frequency in quarter hertz |
| 3 | 1 | detune | signed cents, -100 to 100 |
| 4 | 1 | level | 0 (off) to 127; gain 2^((level - 127) / 8) |
| 5 | 1 | velocity | sensitivity 0 to 7: at 7, velocity 0 is 8 octaves (48.2 dB) quieter than 127, in proportion between |
| 6 | 4 | rates | time codes: attack, decay 1, decay 2, release |
| 10 | 3 | levels | 0 to 127, as level: the attack's peak, the level after decay 1, the level held |

## Units

- **A time code** t, 0 to 127, is 2^(t / 8) ms, from 1 ms to 60.1 s: the
  time a stage takes over its whole range. The attack's range is a gain
  of 0 to 1; the decays' and the release's is 16 octaves (96.3 dB); the
  pitch envelope's 254 levels. A stage that moves only part of its range
  takes that part of the time.
- **A level** step is 2^(1/8), 0.753 dB; 127 is 0 dB.
- **An operator's index**: a modulator at full level moves its carrier's
  phase by 4 pi radians at the most (fm.c, `MOD_SHIFT`); level 103 (a gain
  of 1/8) is index pi/2.
- **Feedback** k (1 to 7) moves the operator's phase by up to
  pi / 2^(7 - k) times the mean of its last two outputs.

## Versions

Version 1 is the first (M5). A reader must refuse a patch with another
magic, version or length, a bad check sum or a field out of range: it
never guesses. A later version will keep the first four bytes' meaning,
so any reader can tell a patch it doesn't know from a damaged one, and
will say here what changed.

/* Startup for the harness's own test images: both stacks below the vector */
/* table, then main(); when main returns, a halt (interrupts off, a jump to */
/* itself), which fwtest reports as `halt`. */
	.section .text.start, "ax"
	.globl _start
_start:
	r0 = 0x01c7e000
	ssp = r0
	r0 = 0x01c7d000
	sp = r0
	usp = r0
	call main
	.globl halt
halt:
	cli
1:	goto 1b
        clang $flags -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1 -c "$n.c" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/start.o" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"
        objdump -d "$out/$n.elf" > "$out/$n.dis"
        rm "$out/$n.o" "$out/$n.elf"
    done
    # blockc exists for the two forms below a base the compiler emits (SR-7)
    if ! grep -q '} = \[-r[0-9]*\]' "$out/blockc.dis" || ! grep -q '\[-r[0-9]*\] = {' "$out/blockc.dis"; then
        echo "blockc: the compiler no longer emits {..} = [-rN] and [-rN] = {..}" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    # rotc exists for the rotate by a register the compiler emits
    if ! grep -q 'r[0-9]* = r[0-9]* <> r[0-9]*$' "$out/rotc.dis"; then
        echo "rotc: the compiler no longer emits rD = rS <> rT" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    for n in $FW_IMAGES; do rm "$out/$n.dis"; done
    for n in $ASM_IMAGES; do
        clang -target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -c "$n.S" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/start.o" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"
        rm "$out/$n.o" "$out/$n.elf"
    done
    for n in $RAW_IMAGES; do
        clang -target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -c "$n.S" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"

#!/bin/bash
# runs the flash test images with the local fwtest build into a new folder $1
S=/tmp/claude-UID/-HOME-Development-[REDACTED:private]-spec/4fc544d9-3a50-4ba0-9cb1-91fc187048df/scratchpad
FW=$S/htarget/debug/fwtest
O=$S/$1
cd ~/Development/[REDACTED:private]/spec/harness
for t in "flashrw --ms 50 --flash tests/data/flash-in.bin --flash-out --ram 0x01c00200:16@end" \
         "flashcall --ms 20 --ram 0x01c00100:4@end" \
         "flashload --ms 20 --ram 0x01c00100:8@end" \
         "flashirq --ms 60 --ram 0x01c00100:0x20@end" \
         "flashkeep --ms 80 --flash-log --flash-out --ram 0x01c00100:8@end"; do
    set -- $t; n=$1; shift
    echo "== $n"
    $FW run tests/images/$n.bin "$@" --out $O/$n 2>&1 | tail -2
done
xxd -e -g4 $O/flashirq/ram-*
head -3 $O/flashkeep/flash-ops.csv; wc -l < $O/flashkeep/flash-ops.csv
xxd -e -g4 $O/flashkeep/ram-*
xxd $O/flashrw/ram-*

content.content:
## Instructions

fwtest runs the code the pinned toolchain's compiler emits for the
firmware's flags (`-target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, tools/build.sh);
the two gaps the checks below found run since 0.4.0. That was checked on a corpus, not proven for
every instruction (SR-7). The corpus: the firmware at `18d9459`, the
vendored Plaits and the demo's C++ built with the firmware's CPU flags,
and several hundred small C functions written to vary types, operations
and pointer patterns, each at `-Os` and `-O2`. Two checks ran in fwtest
0.3.0, each unit on its own:

- every distinct disassembled unit of the corpus's objects (13 981; a
  dual-issue pair is one unit; some are constants in the code, decoded
  as if they were instructions);
- every form in the compiler's assembly output (660, registers and numbers
  abstracted), with each register slot set in turn to r0 to r15 (register
  pairs to each even-odd pair) and each number to values from 0 and ±1 up
  to the 32-bit limits, as far as the assembler accepts them: 34 437
  distinct encodings.

They show only that fwtest decodes and runs each one, not that it
computes what the chip does. An instruction neither check held can still
end a run as a fault ("Outcomes and exit codes"): report it as SR-7 was,
with its bytes and the smallest image that shows it.

No known gaps since fwtest 0.4.0. In 0.3.0 and earlier two forms ended the run as
a fault, "an instruction the emulated CPU cannot decode"; 0.4.0 runs them,
and one more change makes dual-issue pairs behave as the compiler expects:

- **Rotate by a register.** `rD = rS <> rT` (bytes `cc e1`, then two
  bytes naming the registers; `cc f1` as a pair's head), for every
  register. It rotates right by rT: the compiler emits
  `(x << s) | (x >> (32 - s))` as `rT = 32 - rT` then this, and
  `(x >> 7) | (x << 25)` as the rotate by a constant `rD = rS <> 7`. By
  0 it leaves the value (the compiler's masked rotate relies on that). An
  amount of 32 or more is taken mod 32, which the compiler's code doesn't
  show (it masks such amounts itself): don't rely on it.
- **A 4-byte push or pop of any register list.** `[--sp] = {list}` (bytes
  `d8 e8`, then the 16-bit mask, bit k for rk) and `{list} = [sp++]`
  (`d4 e8`, then the mask), without `rets` or `pc`: every list, for
  example `[--sp] = {r5-r1}`, `{r11-r6} = [sp++]` or `{r15} = [sp++]`, as
  the lists from r0 already ran. A push moves sp down by 4 a register and
  the lowest register takes the lowest address; a pop reads them back the
  same way. The compiler emits only lists from r0 (in interrupt
  handlers); lists above r0 behave the same by analogy, not checked
  against the chip.
- **Dual-issue pairs** (`A #` then `B`, as the toolchain's disassembler
  prints them): the pair's second half sees the registers as they were
  before the head, and the head's result is there after the pair. The
  compiler relies on this (in our firmware, a pair whose second half
  stores a byte back through the base register the head changes). In
  0.3.0 and earlier some 4-byte ALU forms as a pair's head wrote their result at
  once, so the second half saw the new value: which ones depended on the
  operation and the registers (of one of each family with the same
  registers, two: `r6 = r5 ^ (1 << r3) #` and `r6 = r5 >>> r3 #`).

None of the three changed any output of the firmware's suite at `cdfd067`.

and pointer patterns, each at `-Os` and `-O2`. Two checks ran in fwtest
0.3.0, each unit on its own:

- every distinct disassembled unit of the corpus's objects (13 981; a
  dual-issue pair is one unit; some are constants in the code, decoded
  as if they were instructions);
- every form in the compiler's assembly output (660, registers and numbers
  abstracted), with each register slot set in turn to r0 to r15 (register
  pairs to each even-odd pair) and each number to values from 0 and ±1 up
  to the 32-bit limits, as far as the assembler accepts them: 34 437
  distinct encodings.

They show only that fwtest decodes and runs each one, not that it
computes what the chip does. An instruction neither check held can still
end a run as a fault ("Outcomes and exit codes"): report it as SR-7 was,
with its bytes and the smallest image that shows it.

No known gaps since fwtest 0.4.0. In 0.3.0 and earlier two forms ended the run as
a fault, "an instruction the emulated CPU cannot decode"; 0.4.0 runs them,
and one more change makes dual-issue pairs behave as the compiler expects:

- **Rotate by a register.** `rD = rS <> rT` (bytes `cc e1`, then two
  bytes naming the registers; `cc f1` as a pair's head), for every
  register. It rotates right by rT: the compiler emits
  `(x << s) | (x >> (32 - s))` as `rT = 32 - rT` then this, and
  `(x >> 7) | (x << 25)` as the rotate by a constant `rD = rS <> 7`. By
  0 it leaves the value (the compiler's masked rotate relies on that). An
  amount of 32 or more is taken mod 32, which the compiler's code doesn't
  show (it masks such amounts itself): don't rely on it.
- **A 4-byte push or pop of any register list.** `[--sp] = {list}` (bytes
  `d8 e8`, then the 16-bit mask, bit k for rk) and `{list} = [sp++]`
  (`d4 e8`, then the mask), without `rets` or `pc`: every list, for
  example `[--sp] = {r5-r1}`, `{r11-r6} = [sp++]` or `{r15} = [sp++]`, as
  the lists from r0 already ran. A push moves sp down by 4 a register and
  the lowest register takes the lowest address; a pop reads them back the
  same way. The compiler emits only lists from r0 (in interrupt
  handlers); lists above r0 behave the same by analogy, not checked
  against the chip.
- **Dual-issue pairs** (`A #` then `B`, as the toolchain's disassembler
  prints them): the pair's second half sees the registers as they were
  before the head, and the head's result is there after the pair. The
  compiler relies on this (in our firmware, a pair whose second half
  stores a byte back through the base register the head changes). In
  0.3.0 and earlier some 4-byte ALU forms as a pair's head wrote their result at
  once, so the second half saw the new value: which ones depended on the
  operation and the registers (of one of each family with the same
  registers, two: `r6 = r5 ^ (1 << r3) #` and `r6 = r5 >>> r3 #`).

None of the three changed any output of the firmware's suite at `cdfd067`.

/* SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT */
/* SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98 */
/* Dual-issue pair heads among the 4-byte ALU forms: one word of each
   family, as itself (byte 1 e0 / e1) and as a pair's head (f0 / f1, which
   the vendor objdump prints with a trailing `#`). The heads are given as
   bytes, since the assembler picks a 2-byte form for some of them; the
   objdump text of each is beside it. Case k keeps three words at
   OUT(3k): the plain form's result; the destination as the pair's second
   half stores it (the value before the pair); and as stored after the
   pair (the head's result). r5 = 0x92345678 and r3 = 5 before each; the
   destination starts at 0x0BADF00D. Then main returns and start.S halts. */
	.text
	.globl main

	.macro case b0, b1, b2, b3, d
	r5 = 0x92345678
	r3 = 5
	\d = 0x0BADF00D
	.byte \b0, \b1, \b2, \b3
	[r7+0] = \d
	r3 = 5
	\d = 0x0BADF00D

/* SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT */
/* SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98 */
/* Dual-issue pairs whose two halves write the same register, as the
   vendor compiler emits them (the four seen in its code, flashkeep.c and
   E-22 at -O2, each a word load of an SPI0 BUF read whose result is unused
   paired after a head computing a value used next): the head's result is
   the one there after the pair. The heads are given as bytes; the objdump
   text of each is beside it. The load reads 0xDEADBEEF from 0x01C01008.
   OUT(k) gets the register after pair k:
   0  r7 = r6 + 0x80000 #, r7 = [r1+8]      r6 = 0x300: 0x00080300
   1  r0 = r1.b0 (u) #, r0 = [r3+8]           r1 = 0x12345678: 0x78
   2  r0 = uextra(r1, p:8, l:8) #, r0 = [r3+8]   0x56
   3  r0 = uextra(r1, p:16, l:8) #, r0 = [r3+8]  0x34
   (fwtest 0.5.0 left 0xDEADBEEF, the second half's value, in each.)
   Then main returns and start.S halts. */
	.text
	.globl main
main:
	r4 = 0x01C00100
	r3 = 0x01C01000
	r2 = 0xDEADBEEF
	[r3+8] = r2

	r1 = 0x01C01000
	r6 = 0x300
	r7 = 0
	.byte 0xe7, 0xf0, 0x00, 0x6a	/* r7 = r6 + 0x80000 # */
	r7 = [r1+8]
	[r4+0] = r7

	r1 = 0x12345678
	r0 = 0
	.byte 0x10, 0xd7		/* r0 = r1.b0 (u) # */
	r0 = [r3+8]
	[r4+4] = r0

	r0 = 0
	.byte 0xb0, 0xf1, 0x20, 0x14	/* r0 = uextra(r1, p:8, l:8) # */
	r0 = [r3+8]
	[r4+8] = r0

	r0 = 0
	.byte 0xb0, 0xf1, 0x20, 0x18	/* r0 = uextra(r1, p:16, l:8) # */
	r0 = [r3+8]
	[r4+12] = r0
	rts
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='build.sh'; s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('ASM_IMAGES="blockmv pairhead rotr pushpop ramcode"','ASM_IMAGES="blockmv pairhead rotr pushpop ramcode pairwaw"')
old='''        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.text"
        objcopy -O binary -j .ramtext "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.ram"'''
new='''        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.text"
        objcopy -O binary -j .ramtext "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.ram"
        objdump -d "$out/$n.elf" > "$out/$n.dis"'''
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)
old='''    for n in $FW_IMAGES; do rm "$out/$n.dis"; done'''
new='''    # pairwaw.S stands for a pair whose halves write one register, which the
    # compiler emits in flashkeep.c (a head, then a load into the same register)
    if ! awk '/ (r[0-9]+) = .*#$/ { split($0, a, "\\t"); h = a[3]; sub(/ =.*/, "", h); gsub(/ /, "", h); next_is = h; next }
              next_is != "" { if ($0 ~ ("\\t[ \\t]*" next_is " = \\\\[")) found = 1; next_is = "" }
              END { exit !found }' "$out/flashkeep.dis"; then
        echo "flashkeep: the compiler no longer pairs a head and a load into one register" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
    for n in $FW_IMAGES $RAM_IMAGES; do rm "$out/$n.dis"; done'''
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

OURS="SHA256SUMS UPSTREAM.md"

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

listed_files() {
    (cd "$DEST" && find . -type f | sed 's|^\./||' | LC_ALL=C sort) | while read -r f; do
        case " $OURS " in *" $f "*) continue ;; esac
        printf '%s\n' "$f"
    done
}

verify() {
    if [ ! -d "$DEST" ]; then
        echo "SKIP: vendor/emulator/ is not on disk (a clean folder leaves it out)"
        return 0
    fi
    status=0
    got=$(sha256 "$SUMS")
    if [ "$got" = "$TREE_SHA256" ]; then echo "OK      SHA256SUMS (tree hash $TREE_SHA256)"
    else echo "CHANGED SHA256SUMS ($got, want $TREE_SHA256)"; status=1; fi
    while read -r want path; do
        [ -n "$want" ] || continue
        if [ ! -f "$DEST/$path" ]; then
            echo "MISSING $path"; status=1; continue
        fi
        [ "$(sha256 "$DEST/$path")" = "$want" ] || { echo "CHANGED $path"; status=1; }
    done < "$SUMS"
    for f in $(listed_files); do
        if ! awk -v p="$f" '$2 == p { found = 1 } END { exit !found }' "$SUMS"; then
            echo "UNLISTED $f"; status=1
        fi
    done
    n=$(grep -c . "$SUMS")
    if [ $status -eq 0 ]; then echo "$n emulator files match commit $UPSTREAM_COMMIT plus patches"; fi
    return $status
}

input.command:
cd ~/Development/[REDACTED:private]/spec; P=vendor/emulator/patches; { cat <<'EOF'
The flash chip on SPI0 as the P25Q80H's datasheet has it (the part whose
JEDEC ID the model answers): an erase or page program needs a write
enable and starts when chip select goes high; a page program wraps
within its 256-byte page (of more than 256 bytes the last 256 count) and
only clears bits; the page (81), 32 KiB (52) and chip (60, C7) erases
join the 4 KiB and 64 KiB ones. Upstream erased on the third address
byte, programmed without a write enable, and ran a program on past the
page's end.

With SpiFlash::timing set (fwtest: the datasheet's maximum times, 3 ms a
program and 12 ms an erase), an operation keeps the chip busy: status 1's
WIP bit reads 1 and WEL stays 1 until it ends, and the chip ignores
every command but the status reads meanwhile (array and ID reads too).
The default timing finishes every operation at once, as upstream did.
The bytes change when an operation starts; SpiFlash::power_cut (and
Soc::power_cut) puts back the part not yet done at that moment, in
proportion to the time gone, so a runner can cut the power during one.
Every operation started is kept in SpiFlash::log (start, end, command,
offset, length). Soc::window_read_busy records the first read of the
code window while the chip is busy (instruction fetches that miss the
decode cache and data reads; not the JIT's direct reads): on the chip
the window can't be served then, and the runner decides what that means
(fwtest ends the run as a fault and also checks each core's pc there).

Our own change (session day-1024, 2026-10-24), from the P25Q80H
datasheet (PROVENANCE P-53) and docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md HW-77 to HW-79.
The crate tests in spiflash.rs and the harness tests flash_capture,
flash_busy_and_the_window and flash_persists_and_power_cuts check it.

EOF
git diff --relative=vendor/emulator -- vendor/emulator/crates/fm1-soc; } > $P/0010-flash-chip-busy-times-and-power-cut.patch
{ cat <<'EOF'
When both halves of a dual-issue pair write the same register, the head's
result is the one there after the pair. Upstream kept the second half's.
The vendor compiler relies on the head's: it pairs a head computing a
value with a word load into the same register whose result it doesn't
use (an unused read of SPI0's BUF), then uses the register as the head's
value, as in

    r7 = r6 + 0x80000  #
    r7 = [r1+8]
    r5 = r7 >> 16

(flash routines at -Os) and `r0 = r1.b0 (u) #` or `r0 = uextra(...) #`
with `r0 = [r3+8]`, then `[r3+8] = r0` (at -O2). Of every pair in the
firmware at main's 6ba587e, the harness's test images and the spec
experiments (at -Os and -O2), these are the only ones whose halves write
one register, and each uses the head's value next; none uses the second
half's. Limit: a head that leaves a register's value as it was can't be
told from one that didn't write it, so the second half's value stays
there.

Our own change (session day-1024, 2026-10-24), from the vendor
toolchain's code (PROVENANCE P-1). The crate test
pair_head_wins_over_its_second_half and the harness test of the same
name (image tests/images/pairwaw.S) fail without it; the firmware's
suite at 6ba587e gives the same outputs with and without it.

EOF
git diff --relative=vendor/emulator -- vendor/emulator/crates/fm1-core; } > $P/0011-pair-head-wins-over-its-second-half.patch
wc -l $P/0010* $P/0011*; sed -n 80,100p tools/fetch-emulator.sh

## The command line

```
fwtest run IMAGE --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest suite FILE --out DIR
fwtest version
```

`run` options:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--ms MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds (up to three decimals). Required. |
| `--out DIR` | Write the outputs here. Required; must be empty or new. |
| `--script FILE` | Timed inputs (below). |
| `--flash FILE` | The flash chip's first bytes (at most 1 MiB); the rest is erased. |
| `--ram ADDR:LEN@WHEN` | Save LEN bytes of memory at ADDR at WHEN. Numbers in decimal, or hex with `0x`. Only RAM (main RAM and the other RAM banks `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` lists) can be saved; anything else is a usage error. Repeatable. |
| `--lcd WHEN` | Save the screen as a PNG at WHEN. Repeatable. |
| `--leds-every MS` | Sample the LEDs every MS into `leds.csv`. |
| `--flash-out` | Save the whole flash chip at the end (`flash.bin`). |
| `--wav` | Save the audio output (`audio.wav`). |
| `--ipb` | Save instructions per audio block (`ipb.csv`). |
| `--console` | Save the bytes written to the chip's debug message register (`console.txt`; `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` names it). |

## Outputs

`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |

| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |

# Upstream note: MIDI out from UART1's transmit side, and the app's CoreMIDI output

For the owner to apply in the F-Emulator app, and to offer to
`joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side only; not filed by a
session. Written in session midi-in-out (2026-10-24) against commit
`43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f`; our copy carries the change as
`vendor/emulator/patches/0009-midi-out-transmit-side.patch` (fwtest 0.5.0).
docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What upstream does

UART1 (`0x12100`) models only the MIDI IN jack's receive DMA. A write of
`TXCNT` (`0x12118`) sets the transmit pending (`CON0` bit 15) at once and
sends nothing ("no TX pin on the board"); a `BUF` (`0x1210C`) write is
plain storage. So a firmware's MIDI out vanishes, and its transmit
interrupt comes the instant it starts a transfer, not 320 µs per byte
later, which hides pacing bugs.

## What the patch does

In `fm1-soc`'s `periph.rs` and `lib.rs`:

- `TXCNT` written: `lib.rs` reads `TXCNT & 0xffff` bytes from `TXADR`
  (`0x12114`, kept in SFR storage) at that moment and hands them to
  `Periph::uart_transmit`. A `BUF` write hands over its low byte.
- `uart_transmit` drops them (counted in `midi_out_dropped()`) when
  `CON0` bit 0 is clear; otherwise it queues them behind anything still
  going. One byte goes per `midi_byte_time()` (10 bits at 31 250 baud:
  76 800 cycles at 240 MHz), whatever `BAUD` says, as the receive side
  does. `next_event` includes the transmitter, so the core never runs or
  skips past a byte's end.
- When the queue empties, `tpnd` is set and `uart_update` raises IRQ 20
  if `CON0` bit 2 is set; the existing `CON0` bit 13 write clears it.
- Every byte sent is kept as `(cycle its stop bit ended, byte)` until
  `Periph::midi_take_sent()` drains them, oldest first.

# Upstream note: the flash chip's busy times, its command rules, and a power cut

For the owner to apply in the F-Emulator app, and to offer to
`joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side only; not filed by a
session. Written in session day-1024 (2026-10-24) against commit
`43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f`; our copy carries the change as
`vendor/emulator/patches/0010-flash-chip-busy-times-and-power-cut.patch`
(fwtest 0.6.0). docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What upstream does

`spiflash.rs` erases a sector as the third address byte arrives, runs a
page program on past the end of its 256-byte page, programs without a
write enable, and finishes every erase and program at once, so the status
register never reads busy. A firmware that forgets the write enable or
the wait, or writes across a page, works in the emulator and not on the
chip.

## What the patch does

In `fm1-soc`'s `spiflash.rs` and `lib.rs`:

- Command rules as the P25Q80H's datasheet gives them (the part whose
  JEDEC ID the model answers): an erase or program needs WREN and starts
  when CS goes high; a program wraps within its page (of more than 256
  bytes the last 256 count) and only clears bits; erases `0x81`, `0x52`,
  `0x60` and `0xC7` join `0x20` and `0xD8`. These hold with or without
  the next item.
- `SpiFlash::timing` (default: none, every operation at once, as now).
  With it, an operation keeps the chip busy for that many cycles: status
  bit 0 (WIP) and bit 1 (WEL) read 1, and every command but `0x05` and
  `0x35` is ignored. `Soc` sets `flash.now` from `periph.cycles` before
  each SPI0 or PD0 access. fwtest sets 3 ms a program and 12 ms an
  erase.
- `SpiFlash::log`: every operation started (start and end cycle, command,
  offset, length). `SpiFlash::power_cut(now)` and `Soc::power_cut()` put
  back the part of an operation in progress not done by then.
- `Soc::window_read_busy`: the first code-window read while the chip is
  busy (fetches that miss the decode cache, and data reads; not the JIT's
  direct reads). fwtest ends the run on it, and checks each core's pc in
  its own copy of the run loops; the app may want to show a warning
  instead, since the stock firmware's behaviour on the chip is to keep
  its flash routines and handlers in RAM.

## For the app

The rules in the first item change what a firmware sees only when it
breaks them. The busy time is opt-in (`timing`). Whether the app turns it
on, and what it does about window reads while busy, is the owner's
choice; with it on, the stock firmware and community firmwares must keep
their flash routines in RAM, as they do on the chip.
EOF

# Upstream note: a dual-issue pair whose halves write one register

For the owner to apply in the F-Emulator app, and to offer to
`joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side only; not filed by a
session. Written in session day-1024 (2026-10-24) against commit
`43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f`; our copy carries the change as
`vendor/emulator/patches/0011-pair-head-wins-over-its-second-half.patch`
(fwtest 0.6.0). docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What upstream does

`fm1-core` holds a pair head's register results until the second half has
run, then commits those the second half didn't change. When both halves
write the same register, the second half's value stays.

## What the vendor compiler expects

The head's. It pairs a head computing a value with a word load into the
same register whose result it doesn't use, then uses the register as the
head's value:

```
r7 = r6 + 0x80000  #
r7 = [r1+8]
r5 = r7 >> 16
```

(an unused read of SPI0's `BUF` in a flash routine at `-Os`; at `-O2` also
`r0 = r1.b0 (u) #` and `r0 = uextra(r1, p:8, l:8) #` with `r0 = [r3+8]`,
then `[r3+8] = r0`). In everything we compiled, these are the only pairs
whose halves write one register, and each uses the head's value next.

## What the patch does

Both commit loops (`step` and `exec_fast_paired`) commit every register
the head changed, over the second half's write. A head that leaves a
register's value as it was can't be told from one that didn't write it;
then the second half's value stays. Crate test
`pair_head_wins_over_its_second_half`; fwtest's harness test of the same
name. fwtest's firmware suite gives the same outputs with and without it.

# Upstream note: the flash chip's busy times, its command rules, and a power cut

For the owner to apply in the F-Emulator app, and to offer to
`joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side only; not filed by a
session. Written in session day-1024 (2026-10-24) against commit
`43ed5580064885e93bc8d20be931ae950d10cd4f`; our copy carries the change as
`vendor/emulator/patches/0010-flash-chip-busy-times-and-power-cut.patch`
(fwtest 0.6.0). docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What upstream does

`spiflash.rs` erases a sector as the third address byte arrives, runs a
page program on past the end of its 256-byte page, programs without a
write enable, and finishes every erase and program at once, so the status
register never reads busy. A firmware that forgets the write enable or
the wait, or writes across a page, works in the emulator and not on the
chip.

## What the patch does

In `fm1-soc`'s `spiflash.rs` and `lib.rs`:

- Command rules as the P25Q80H's datasheet gives them (the part whose
  JEDEC ID the model answers): an erase or program needs WREN and starts
  when CS goes high; a program wraps within its page (of more than 256
  bytes the last 256 count) and only clears bits; erases `0x81`, `0x52`,
  `0x60` and `0xC7` join `0x20` and `0xD8`. These hold with or without
  the next item.
- `SpiFlash::timing` (default: none, every operation at once, as now).
  With it, an operation keeps the chip busy for that many cycles: status
  bit 0 (WIP) and bit 1 (WEL) read 1, and every command but `0x05` and
  `0x35` is ignored. `Soc` sets `flash.now` from `periph.cycles` before
  each SPI0 or PD0 access. fwtest sets 3 ms a program and 12 ms an
  erase.
- `SpiFlash::log`: every operation started (start and end cycle, command,
  offset, length). `SpiFlash::power_cut(now)` and `Soc::power_cut()` put
  back the part of an operation in progress not done by then.
- `Soc::window_read_busy`: the first code-window read while the chip is
  busy (fetches that miss the decode cache, and data reads; not the JIT's
  direct reads). fwtest ends the run on it, and checks each core's pc in
  its own copy of the run loops; the app may want to show a warning
  instead, since the stock firmware's behaviour on the chip is to keep
  its flash routines and handlers in RAM.

## For the app

The rules in the first item change what a firmware sees only when it
breaks them. The busy time is opt-in (`timing`). Whether the app turns it
on, and what it does about window reads while busy, is the owner's
choice; with it on, the stock firmware and community firmwares must keep
their flash routines in RAM, as they do on the chip.
EOF

# Upstream note: a dual-issue pair whose halves write one register

For the owner to apply in the F-Emulator app, and to offer to
`joakimeriksson/fm1-emu` if wanted. Spec side only; not filed by a
session. Written in session day-1024 (2026-10-24) against commit

`vendor/emulator/patches/0011-pair-head-wins-over-its-second-half.patch`
(fwtest 0.6.0). docs/EMULATOR-PARITY.md lists it.

## What upstream does

`fm1-core` holds a pair head's register results until the second half has
run, then commits those the second half didn't change. When both halves
write the same register, the second half's value stays.

## What the vendor compiler expects

The head's. It pairs a head computing a value with a word load into the
same register whose result it doesn't use, then uses the register as the
head's value:

```
r7 = r6 + 0x80000  #
r7 = [r1+8]
r5 = r7 >> 16
```

(an unused read of SPI0's `BUF` in a flash routine at `-Os`; at `-O2` also
`r0 = r1.b0 (u) #` and `r0 = uextra(r1, p:8, l:8) #` with `r0 = [r3+8]`,
then `[r3+8] = r0`). In everything we compiled, these are the only pairs
whose halves write one register, and each uses the head's value next.

## What the patch does

Both commit loops (`step` and `exec_fast_paired`) commit every register
the head changed, over the second half's write. A head that leaves a
register's value as it was can't be told from one that didn't write it;
then the second half's value stays. Crate test
`pair_head_wins_over_its_second_half`; fwtest's harness test of the same
name. fwtest's firmware suite gives the same outputs with and without it.

**What:** fwtest 0.6.0, for M7.
- **Vendor patch 0010, the flash chip.** It follows the P25Q80H's command rules: an erase or program needs a write enable and starts when chip select goes high, a program wraps within its 256-byte page, and the 256-byte, 32 KiB and whole-chip erases now work. fwtest sets the datasheet's maximum busy times: 3 ms a program, 12 ms an erase. While busy, the status register reports busy and the chip ignores every other command. The patch also adds an operations log and a power cut that keeps the part already done.
- **The code window while busy.** fwtest ends the run as a fault when either core runs or reads the code window while the chip is busy. New options `--power-cut MS` and `--flash-log`, and a new `power-cut` outcome (exit 0).
- **Vendor patch 0011, pairs writing one register.** When both halves of a dual-issue pair write the same register, the head's result is kept, as the vendor compiler's code expects. 0.5.0 kept the second half's value, so a flash driver's unused BUF reads computed wrong addresses.
- **Tests.** New test images with flash routines in RAM, `pairwaw.S`, harness tests and suite cases.
- **Spec.** E-22 now runs its routines from RAM and is re-run; HW-83 supersedes HW-47 and HW-82.
- **Docs.** HARNESS.md ("The flash chip", options, outputs, outcomes, "Instructions", versions), EMULATOR-PARITY.md rows 0010 and 0011, and two upstream notes for the app.

**Why:** M7 and SR-9 need these tests: flash that persists from run to run (this already worked through `--flash`/`--flash-out`), a power cut in the middle of a write, and audio that keeps going through an erase. Those need a chip that is busy the way the real one is. 0011 fixes the gap #97 names in HARNESS.md.

**How:** See the commit. The window check lives in fwtest's own copies of upstream's run loops, which run one block at a time while the chip is busy. The evidence for 0011: every pair whose halves write the same register, in the firmware at `6ba587e`, the harness test images and the spec experiments, uses the head's value next.

**Pin:** this needs a follow-up pull request after the merge. `fwtest-image` publishes from main, and the digest then goes into `config/fwtest-image`. Until that pin, the clean side keeps 0.5.0.
